name: Mathletics
line: Mathletics practices in activities, quests and races. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Mathletics: Mathletics practices in activities, quests and races. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Mathletics practices math in activities aligned to the curriculum, Skill Quests grouped by standard and timed races, and at school the teacher assigns content to ability groups [2][5][8]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. Every answer, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. The Mathletics Skill Quests page describes no placement test [5]. Its New Courses include a diagnostic test and unit practice tests [6], and at school the teacher sets up ability groups and assigns content to each [8].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Mathletics the unit is the activity, a set of ten steps aligned to the curriculum [2]. Its teaching comes as animated tutorials and audio in elementary content, printable eBooks in secondary, and conceptual and activity videos [7][3]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [13].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Mathletics moves a learner on in Skill Quests after mastery of earlier topics is shown, and the page does not say what counts as mastery [5].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Mathletics Skill Quests group questions by curriculum standard [5]. We found no scheduled return to earlier skills in the pages we read [5][6][7]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [12].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, so a learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. It runs from counting through precalculus on one map of skills. At school, the Mathletics teacher places students in ability groups and assigns content to each group [8]. Its U.S. alignment covers kindergarten to grade 8, plus Algebra I and Integrated Math III [4].

rows.range: Ages 5 to 16 [1]. U.S. alignment: kindergarten to grade 8, plus Algebra I and Integrated Math III [4].
rows.start: No placement test described for Skill Quests [5]. Its New Courses include a diagnostic test [6].
rows.teaching: Animated tutorials and audio in elementary content, printable eBooks in secondary, and conceptual and activity videos [7][3].
rows.next: Skill Quests by curriculum standard, and adaptive activities [5][7]. At school, the teacher assigns content to ability groups [8].
rows.mastery: Skill Quests move on after mastery is shown. The page gives no rule for it [5].
rows.review: None found in the pages we read [5][6][7].
rows.print: A library of printable worksheets with solutions [2].
rows.adult: At school, the teacher sets ability groups, assigns content and reviews reports [8].
rows.reports: Real-time marking and reports from the learner up to the district [3]. A parent dashboard [2].
rows.evidence: Evidence for ESSA gives no rating: qualifying studies found no significant positive outcomes [10]. The site claims ESSA Level II certification, naming no certifier [4].

theirs: Mathletics is an online math program from 3P Learning [9], built for learners aged 5 to 16 [1][2]. In the United States it is aligned to standards from kindergarten through grade 8, plus Algebra I and Integrated Math III [4].

A learner works through activities of ten steps aligned to the curriculum, Skill Quests that group questions by standard, and games such as Live Mathletics, a timed race against other learners [2][5]. Skill Quests move a learner on after mastery is shown [5]. Elementary content has animated tutorials and audio; secondary content has adaptive practice and printable eBooks [7]. Correct answers earn points toward a weekly certificate [6]. At school, the teacher sets up ability groups and assigns content [8].
credit: Timed fact practice. Live Mathletics races learners against each other [2], and regular timed activities to build fluency are one of six recommendations rated strong evidence in the What Works Clearinghouse guide for elementary students who struggle in math [14].
Skill Quests move a learner on only after mastery of earlier topics is shown [5].
Animated tutorials and audio support in elementary content [7].

theirs: The Mathletics U.S. standards page says the program is "Certified under ESSA Level II". It names no certifying body and links no report [4]. The home, About, standards and schools pages we read cite no study [1][4][7][9].

Evidence for ESSA, the Johns Hopkins clearinghouse, lists Mathletics without a rating. Its summary reads: "Qualifying studies found no significant positive outcomes" [10]. Mathletics has no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [11].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on a test the researchers wrote, against 38% for practice in blocks [12]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve math performance [13]. AMP's problems carry worked examples, and learned skills come back mixed with other math at growing intervals.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want timed fact practice, with races against other learners.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back, mixed with other math.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want one program from counting through precalculus.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Mathletics?
questions.answer: Mathletics practices in activities aligned to the curriculum, Skill Quests grouped by standard and timed races, and at school the teacher assigns content to ability groups [2][5][8]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Mathletics work?
questions.answer: Evidence for ESSA lists Mathletics without a rating: the studies that qualified found no significant positive outcomes [10]. Its site says it is certified under ESSA Level II, and names no certifying body and links no study [4].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
